body: Eleven people came tonight; last week it was nine. A Tuesday in February, and a man is stacking their chairs in a church hall that smells of instant coffee and damp carpet. On the whiteboard behind him there is a list in three colours of marker — a scan on Thursday, a tribunal in March, a boy who has stopped speaking to his mother — and the list is longer than it was in September, not shorter. He rubs none of it off. He puts the urn away, turns the strip lights out in the order they have always been turned out, and locks the door on the nineteenth week of a prayer meeting that has produced nothing anybody could point to.

Nothing anybody could point to is not the same as nothing. It feels identical from the inside, though, and that particular feeling is the ordinary condition of most serious believers for most of their lives.
Acts 2 is one of the most preached chapters in the book. Acts 1 is the setup nobody lingers on, which is unfortunate, because Acts 1 contains the part that most listeners are currently living in.

Take the arithmetic literally for a moment, because the tradition named after the fire almost never does. The instruction is given. The ascension happens. Then the room fills with wind and flame on the day of Pentecost, and between those two events sits an interval with nothing in it — no signs, no confirmations, no interim bulletin explaining the delay. The text hands that interval a handful of verses, and what it records them doing is entirely unremarkable: they prayed, they stayed together, and they dealt with a piece of unglamorous administrative business about replacing a man who had betrayed them. Ten days of that, and then one day of fire. The movement took its name from the one day.

This band runs from HM 300.30 to HM 398.70 and carries 121 stations, of which 46 are on air. Two of them sit directly on this beat. HM 350.00 is The Upper Room, and the number is not an accident: fifty is the count from the sheaf to the fiftieth day, so the station named after the room sits on the number of what happened in it. It is on air, carrying sung Scripture prayer continuously. HM 341.90 Pentecostal Fire is assigned and still in build.

What the interval actually cost the people inside it is worth stating without decoration. They were told to wait, with no date given, in a city that had recently executed their teacher, by a man who had then left. They were a group that had very publicly failed him. Nothing inside that room could confirm that the instruction had not simply been misheard, and every morning of those ten days was a fresh decision to stay somewhere that staying was dangerous while nothing whatever happened. The waiting is not the preamble. It is most of the account.

A tradition that celebrates the fire ought to be the best in the world at teaching the ten days, and mostly it is not. What gets recorded, shared and preached is the moment: the aisle, the collapse, the phone held up at the back of the room. The lead-up is edited out because it is unwatchable — it is somebody being faithful in an empty week. So the people who most need a theology of the interval are handed a highlight reel of everybody else’s arrivals, and they draw the only conclusion available to them, which is that something has gone wrong with them personally.

This is why the beat is arranged the way it is. The fire stations are here and they are meant to be here. Alongside them sit prayer frequencies that do nothing but pray, and ordinary continuous worship stations built to be left running through a flat Wednesday. Learn roughly where those sit and you have learned the actual shape of a life with God in it, which is a small number of extraordinary hours held up by an enormous number of ordinary ones.
The alternative is to organise your whole spiritual life around the next event. A great many people do, and it works beautifully for about a fortnight afterwards.

Be fair to the event first. Something genuinely happens at conferences and camps and revival meetings; people are converted there, healed there, and set on a course they hold for forty years. Anybody who has been in one knows the difference between the hype and the real thing, and both are present in the same room. But an event cannot do the ten days for you, because the ten days are not an event — they are the absence of one. The gathering ends on the Sunday afternoon and the person goes back to a Tuesday, and nothing they were given on the Sunday was designed for a Tuesday. What they needed was not more Sunday. It was a way to stay.
The fire is not the reproducible part. The waiting is.

A girl of sixteen prays for her father every night before she goes to sleep, and has done since she was twelve. It started as something urgent. It is now something she does while her phone charges, in the dark, in about forty seconds, using the same six words she has always used, because she gave up looking for new ones a long time ago. She does not expect anything in particular. She would not say she has faith about it exactly; she would say she has not stopped. Her father is not better. He is not worse either. On the four hundredth night, or the eight hundredth — nobody is counting, which is rather the point — she says the six words, turns over, and goes to sleep.
That is what obedience looks like with no result attached to it, and it is by far the most common form of it. It is also, on the evidence of the text, the form the fire tends to fall on.

There is a real danger in all of this and it should be said plainly. A theology of waiting can be used to excuse a church that has quietly stopped expecting anything at all, and to sanctify a deadness that is nobody’s cross but its own. Some waiting is disobedience with better manners. Ten days of prayer is not the same thing as ten years of a habit nobody in the building believes in any more, and pretending otherwise is how congregations die comfortably.

Which means the distinction is not patience against impatience. It is whether the waiting is being done in the room. The people in Acts 1 waited together, in one place, doing the small ordinary things — praying, staying, sorting out who was in — and they were still there when it happened. Waiting that keeps you in the room is faith. Waiting that lets you leave it quietly, one Tuesday at a time, is something else entirely, and the difference is visible from outside long before it is visible from inside.

So the ten days are not the throat-clearing before the story. They are the largest part of it by duration, the only part almost anybody reading this is currently in, and the part on which the one day depends. A tradition that preaches only the second chapter is teaching its own people to despise the exact conditions they will spend most of their lives in. Correcting that is not a lowering of expectation. It is where expectation is kept alive between arrivals.
All of which is theology until something is actually playing in the room while you are doing the washing-up.

The dial carries four kinds of programming and it helps to know they are there before you start turning. There is music, which is most of it. There is teaching and prayer, where the Word is opened and prayed through rather than sung. There is family programming, which is simply safe to leave running in a room with children in it. And there are the international stations — 40 of them across 29 languages, hosted in those languages rather than dubbed into them afterwards. None of it asks what you are in the mood for, which in a nineteenth week is a mercy rather than a limitation.

If you want somewhere to start, start at HM 303.10 — Yes and Amen. It is on air now, and it is covenant worship: declaration records built on the line that every promise of God is Yes and Amen in Him. Which means that almost everything on it is about promises — promises made, promises held, promises not yet visibly kept. That is a strange thing to have running in a kitchen right up until you are in the interval, at which point it is close to the only thing worth having on. It will not tell you the wait is nearly over, because it does not know and neither does anybody else. What it does is keep saying, in somebody else’s voice, at a volume you can talk over, that the promise was made by someone who has never been in the habit of forgetting.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone or laptop is nearest, press play, and it plays — it is built deliberately for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have. If you would like it nearer to hand, add the page to your home screen and it will open like anything else on it. And do make yourself an account while you are there. It is free, it keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band finds out which frequencies people are actually reaching for — which is how the next one gets built, and how the silent ones get filled.

So put it on this week rather than deciding about it. Put it on for the drive, for the hour after the meeting when the hall is empty and the chairs are going back on the trolley, for the forty seconds before the phone finishes charging. Do not wait until you feel something first, because feeling something is the one part you cannot arrange, and it was never the part you were asked for. You were asked to stay in the room. This is one small way of staying in it with the sound on.
